薩羅德琴為弦鳴樂器，Hornbostel–Sachs 編號 321.321-6。: The sarod is a chordophone, Hornbostel–Sachs number 321.321-6. The source mentions a body of teak with the soundbox covered in goatskin; the fretboard is usually stainless steel, sometimes chrome-plated or nickel-plated cast steel. The strings are steel or phosphor bronze, and the early modifications brought in metal strings and an iron plate. The pick is triangular and may be made of polished coconut shell, ebony, cocobolo, horn, cattle bone or Delrin; early ones used bare metal wire. The materials of the other parts are not stated.
薩羅德琴為撥奏弦鳴樂器，發聲以右手持三角形撥片撥弦。因無品，左手須將弦用力壓向指: The sarod is a plucked chordophone: the right hand holds a triangular pick and plucks the strings. Because there are no frets, the left hand must press the string firmly against the fretboard to stop a note and to make a continuous slide (meend). The string can be stopped with the tip of a fingernail, or with nail and fingertip together; the basic order of operations is to pluck first and then stop, and to practise coordinating the slide with the pluck.
薩羅德琴用於北印度古典音樂，常與錫塔琴並列為主要撥弦樂器；在德魯帕德與基亞爾風格: The sarod is used in North Indian classical music and is usually named alongside the sitar as one of its main plucked instruments; in the dhrupad and khyal styles the metal strings and metal fretboard make it easier to sustain long tones and fine ornament. The source also mentions that it entered court music at Lucknow, Gwalior and Rewa, and that it is connected with raga performance.
薩羅德琴用於北印度古典音樂，起源不明確，學者追溯至印度薩拉迪亞維納、南印度薩拉瓦: The sarod is used in North Indian classical music and its origin is not clear; scholars trace it to the Indian saradiya veena, the South Indian Sarasvat veena or the Afghan rubab. Its name may have come from Persia in the late Mughal empire, meaning song or melody. In the early nineteenth century it may have developed from the Afghan rubab and been popular among Pashtun communities east of Delhi; later players added metal strings and a metal plate, which made ornament easier in dhrupad and khyal. The present form was settled in the 1850s and was valued at Rewa, Shahjahanpur, Gwalior and Lucknow. From 1855 Niamatullah Khan removed the frets, added an iron plate and changed to metal strings; in the twentieth century Allauddin Khan and Ayet Ali Khan added drone strings and sympathetic strings.
薩羅德琴音色沉鬱深邃，帶有溫暖的金屬質感。其音域偏低中音域，聲音內斂而富有表現力: The sarod's timbre is sombre and deep, with a warm metallic quality. Its range lies in the lower middle register, and the sound is inward and expressive. Because the fretboard is stainless steel, the left-hand fingernail produces a distinctive metallic sheen against the string, so the timbre keeps its warmth while gaining a certain tensile hardness. The goatskin soundbox and the many sympathetic strings give thick overtones and a full, layered sound. Against the bright clarity of the sitar the sarod is lower and more inward; against the cello it has the extra character of metal. The fretless design allows wide slides, and its changes of colour are fine and continuous, which suits the complex, subtle expression of North Indian classical music.

The sarod is a plucked lute commonly used in the North Indian classical music of the South Asian subcontinent, a chordophone, Hornbostel–Sachs number 321.321-6. The body is fretless, the fretboard is usually metal, and the soundbox is covered in goatskin; it usually carries four or five main melody strings, two drone strings and nine to eleven sympathetic strings, is played with a pick, and the left hand can slide continuously along the strings. Its timbre is low and inward, with resonant aftertones; it was once played by court musicians, and it is usually named with the sitar as the most representative instrument of that music.
